stories.title: Jakarta's Airports Reopen — But Travel Chaos Isn't Over Yet
stories.headline_kid: The airports shut down by volcano ash have finally reopened, but getting a flight is still a headache for many travellers!
summary: Remember the volcano ash that grounded flights near Jakarta over the weekend? Good news — Jakarta's main airport and several others have now reopened. A volcano called Anak Krakatau erupted and threw huge clouds of ash into the sky. Ash is dangerous for planes because tiny bits of rock and glass can damage jet engines, a bit like sand jamming up a fan.

Eight airports had to close because of this, cancelling almost 3,000 flights and leaving more than 340,000 passengers stuck, unable to reach home or their holiday plans. That's roughly the population of a small town, all waiting anxiously at airports!

Even though the airports have reopened, the trouble isn't over. So many people are still trying to travel that flight tickets have become very expensive, and train tickets have completely sold out. Some travellers are being forced to take long, tiring overland journeys instead of a quick flight.

For Singapore, this matters because many families fly to Indonesia for holidays or to visit relatives. If you or someone you know has a trip to Indonesia planned soon, there could still be delays or higher prices for a while as things slowly get back to normal.

lenses.me: If your family has a trip to Indonesia planned, you might face a longer wait or a pricier ticket than usual.
lenses.family: Parents may need to rebook flights or pay more for train or bus tickets if their travel plans were affected.
lenses.friends: Some classmates might have relatives stuck in Indonesia or stories about postponed holidays to share.
lenses.nation: Singapore's airport and airlines like SIA often work closely with Indonesia's airports, so disruptions there can affect flight schedules here too.
lenses.world: This shows how one volcano can create a domino effect, disrupting travel and daily life for hundreds of thousands of people across a whole region.

stories.title: Sarawak's Haze Emergency Is Lifted — But the Air Is Still Not Fully Clean
stories.headline_kid: Malaysia has ended its emergency over the terrible haze in Sarawak, but the air there is still not completely safe to breathe.
summary: A few days ago, Malaysia declared an emergency in the Serian district of Sarawak because the haze there had become so thick it was considered dangerous to health. Now, the government has lifted that emergency after checking that the air quality had dropped back below hazardous levels.

This decision was approved by Malaysia's King, based on advice from the Prime Minister and Sarawak's leader. It's a bit like a doctor saying a patient is no longer in critical condition, but still needs rest and care.

Even though the emergency is over, officials warned that health risks remain. This means people in the area should still be careful, especially those with breathing problems, and avoid too much time outdoors.

This matters to families in Singapore too, because haze from fires in Indonesia and Malaysia has drifted over to our skies in recent weeks. Any improvement in the region is good news, but it doesn't mean the haze problem is completely solved.

lenses.me: You might still need to check the air quality app before playing outdoor sports, just in case haze drifts over Singapore again.
lenses.family: Parents may keep monitoring the PSI readings and keep masks or air purifiers ready at home.
lenses.friends: Outdoor CCAs or school events could still be affected if the haze situation changes suddenly.
lenses.nation: Singapore's National Environment Agency continues to track the haze closely and may issue advisories if conditions worsen again.
lenses.world: This shows how neighbouring countries need to work together, since haze doesn't stop at borders — it's a shared problem needing shared solutions.

stories.title: Sembawang Shipyard Sails Into History — Homes to Rise on Its Old Grounds
stories.headline_kid: One of Singapore's oldest shipyards is closing down after decades of fixing giant ships — and homes will be built there instead.
summary: Sembawang Shipyard, now called Seatrium Admiralty Yard, has been repairing and building ships for almost a hundred years. Think of it as a giant hospital for ships — when huge vessels needed fixing, they came here to be patched up before sailing off again.
Now, the shipyard is winding down its operations for good. This means the machines are slowing to a stop, and the workers who have spent years there are saying goodbye to a place full of memories.

The land will eventually be redeveloped into new housing, part of Singapore's plan to make space for more homes as our population grows. It's a bit like turning an old factory into a brand-new neighbourhood with parks and flats.

Long-time employees shared bittersweet feelings with reporters — proud of the yard's rich history, but hopeful that the new development will still remember its maritime roots and the people who worked hard there.

lenses.me: One day, new flats or parks might stand where giant ships used to be repaired — maybe you'll even live near there someday!
lenses.family: If anyone in your family works in shipping or the marine industry, this story shows how Singapore's economy is always changing.
lenses.friends: You and your friends could visit the redeveloped area someday and learn about its shipbuilding history through murals or museums.
lenses.nation: This shows how Singapore reuses land wisely, turning old industrial sites into new homes as the country continues to grow.
lenses.world: It reflects a bigger trend around the world, where cities transform old industrial areas into modern housing to meet changing needs.

stories.title: China Says No to Fake AI Videos of Real People
stories.headline_kid: China's top court just made new rules saying people can't use AI to copy someone's face or voice without asking first.
summary: China's highest court has released new guidelines about a tricky problem: deepfakes. A deepfake is when computer programmes use artificial intelligence (AI) to create a video or audio clip that looks and sounds exactly like a real person — even if that person never said or did those things. Imagine a very convincing digital "costume" that lets a computer wear someone else's face and voice.

The new rules say people cannot create or share these fake clones of someone's face or voice without getting their permission first. This is meant to stop people from being tricked, embarrassed, or even scammed by fake videos that look real.

This matters far beyond China. Around the world, including in Singapore, scammers have used fake voices to trick people into believing they were talking to a family member or bank staff, asking for money. Singapore has also been stepping up efforts to fight online scams and protect people from being fooled by fake digital content.
As AI tools become easier to use, more countries may create similar rules. It's a good reminder for all of us — including kids — to think twice before believing everything we see or hear online.

lenses.me: Not everything you see or hear online is real — always check with a trusted adult if something looks suspicious.
lenses.family: Parents and grandparents should be extra careful of phone calls or videos that seem to be from family members but might actually be AI fakes.
lenses.friends: You and your classmates can talk about how to spot deepfakes, like unnatural mouth movements or strange voices.
lenses.nation: Singapore is also working hard to protect citizens from scams that use fake AI voices and videos.
lenses.world: This shows countries around the world are racing to create rules to keep up with fast-changing AI technology.

stories.title: Piano Star Niu Niu Takes On a Massive Musical Challenge — For a Great Cause
stories.headline_kid: A famous young pianist is playing eight big pieces of music in one night in Singapore, all to raise money for kids with cancer!
summary: Niu Niu, a pianist from China who was once a child prodigy (someone incredibly talented at a very young age), is preparing for one of the biggest challenges of his career. He will perform highlights from eight major musical works in a single concert in Singapore — a bit like running eight mini marathons back-to-back instead of just one!
The concert, happening on 27 October, will even feature him playing two different instruments and blending Eastern and Western music styles together.
This special performance is for a wonderful cause: it will help raise funds for Viva Foundation, a charity that supports children with cancer, as the organisation celebrates its 20th anniversary.
Niu Niu's dedication shows how talent and hard work can be used to help others. It's a great reminder that even something as fun as music can make a real difference in someone's life.

lenses.me: This story might inspire you to think about how your own talents — music, art, or sports — could one day help others.
lenses.family: Your family could consider supporting or attending charity concerts like this one to help children in need.
lenses.friends: You and your friends could talk about how music brings people together for good causes.
lenses.nation: Singapore often hosts international artists for charity events, showing how the arts scene here supports meaningful causes.
lenses.world: It shows how music and kindness can cross borders, uniting people from different countries for a shared good cause.
